title: What is Collective Hysteria?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain collective hysteria, also called mass psychogenic disorder (MPD) or mass psychosomatic reaction: outbreaks of real physical symptoms with no toxic cause, usually spreading among groups in rigid settings like schools. They cover a 2000s Mexico girls' boarding school outbreak, a Tennessee school case documented in the New England Journal of Medicine, historical cases such as the 1518 Strasbourg dancing plague and Medieval dancing mania, the Salem witch trials, and the gender bias in diagnosis. They discuss the nocebo effect (contrasted with the placebo effect), the cholecystokinin hormone study by Fabrizio Benedetti, the New Zealand Eltroxin pill change and media-driven adverse-event reports, the Corinth, New York Tourette-like outbreak, the Riverside "toxic lady" Gloria Ramirez case, sick building syndrome, and the ethical problem for doctors of what to tell patients. The episode ends with listener mail from Jason Flack about his late twin sister and epilepsy, and a promise of a future epilepsy show.

segments.title: Opening banter and diagnosis joke
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke around, and Chuck says he feels nauseous and dizzy, like others in the office. Josh introduces collective hysteria, also called mass psychogenic disorder, and discusses why the word hysteria is objectionable.

segments.title: Mexico boarding school outbreak and definition
segments.summary: A girls' boarding school in Chalco, Mexico had an outbreak of vomiting, fever, nausea and trouble walking. Ten days of Christmas break did not stop it, and no toxin was found. The hosts list alternate names and note that symptoms are physically real, citing Timothy F. Jones's 2000 article. About eighty historical cases are documented, and the NIH reportedly gets about two per week.

segments.title: History, gender bias and young females
segments.summary: Historical examples include the medieval dancing mania and the Salem witch trials. The condition more often affects teenage girls, which the hosts link to the hysteria label and to a theory about girls' repression, referencing Beatlemania. A British case of cucumbers in school lunches shows why physicians must avoid diagnosing from demographics alone.

segments.title: Diagnosis, risk factors and Tennessee school case
segments.summary: The hosts describe how an outbreak looks like an epidemic, and the difficulty of testing without over-testing. Risk factors include isolated communities, rigid structured settings, and schools, with top-down spread from a teacher or older student. A Tennessee school case from the New England Journal of Medicine involved a gas odor, about 180 people taken to the emergency room, a two-week closure, and recovery after the outbreak was traced to mass psychogenic disorder.

segments.title: Nocebo effect and the cholecystokinin study
segments.summary: The nocebo effect is defined as the opposite of the placebo effect, where expecting harm causes harm. The hosts describe the rose allergy story and research by Fabrizio Benedetti. Benedetti found that a saline injection described as painful increased reported pain, but blocking cholecystokinin removed that effect.

segments.title: Electromagnetic sensitivity, gluten and the Eltroxin case
segments.summary: The hosts mention the film Safe and Debbie Bird, a London woman who says she has electromagnetic sensitivity. They then discuss gluten sensitivity as possible collective belief. In New Zealand in 2007, a hormone replacement drug Eltroxin changed in appearance, and reported side effects grew, rising sharply as media coverage increased. Pill color and perceived drowsiness are also discussed.

segments.title: Belief and health, positive mental attitude, and sick building syndrome
segments.summary: A study found that women who believed they were prone to heart disease died at four times the rate of women with identical risk factors. Josh describes getting sick after a tour trip, linking it to his mind. The hosts then discuss sick building syndrome, which may be linked more to job stress than to ventilation.

segments.title: Doctor disclosure ethics and Corinth, New York case
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the ethical problem of what doctors should tell patients about possible side effects. They suggest framing risks as percentages and avoiding naming illnesses. They then describe the Corinth, New York case, where Laurie Brounwell's Tourette-like symptoms after a concert were followed by 14 other students. Erin Brockovich was reportedly involved, and the hosts note no legitimate effects were found.

segments.title: Riverside toxic lady and dancing plague
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Riverside, California case of Gloria Ramirez, where medical staff fell ill while treating her. Health officials first called it mass hysteria, but a later explanation pointed to a skin salve. They then describe the 1518 Strasbourg dancing plague, with dancers and deaths, and possible explanations of ergot poisoning and mass psychosis.

segments.title: Listener mail on grief and epilepsy
segments.summary: Listener Jason Flack writes about losing his fraternal twin sister Jessica in 2010 to sudden unexplained death in epilepsy (SUDEP), and shares comic-style artwork. Josh and Chuck express sympathy and promise a future epilepsy show.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give information on how to contact the show and end the episode.
